title: Damping Off: How to Spot It and Save Your Seedlings
metaTitle: Damping Off: Signs, Causes and Control in Seedbeds
metaDescription: Damping off makes seeds rot and seedlings collapse at the soil line in wet seedbeds. Learn the signs and the clean seedbed steps that stop it.
excerpt: Damping off is the disease that makes seeds rot before they sprout and seedlings fall over at the soil line. It is the most common reason a seedbed of tomato, talong or pechay suddenly thins out.

heroImage.alt: A young seedling with a thin, pinched stem near the root, the sign of damping off
heroImage.credit: INAKAvillage211, CC BY SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Damping off is a group of diseases, caused mostly by Pythium and Rhizoctonia, with Phytophthora and Fusarium also involved. The Pacific Pests and Pathogens database says these organisms occur widely in soil. They survive on organic matter and plant roots. They are everywhere, which is the bad news. The good news is that they only strike weak, wet or overcrowded seedlings.

The damage is quick, so the seedbed is where you win or lose. A few days of waterlogged soil can wipe out many seedlings, and a bad seedbed wastes your seed money. Read our guide to [vegetables in the Philippines](/crops/vegetables-philippines) for seedbed basics. See also how a similar soil problem, [bacterial wilt](/diseases/bacterial-wilt), kills older plants.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Pythium spp., Rhizoctonia solani, Fusarium spp.
Vegetable seedlings (tomato, eggplant, pepper, cabbage and others), also other crops raised from seed
Damping off hits seeds in the soil and seedlings in their first two weeks, and it is worst in cold or waterlogged, wet seedbeds.
The fungi and water molds live in the soil and in organic matter. They move by water splash, contaminated tools, infected potting media and roots.

blocks.text: Look at the seedbed in the first two weeks. Pre emergence damping off leaves gaps in the row, because the seeds rot before they sprout. Post emergence damping off leaves seedlings that fall over, with a thin, water soaked, discolored stem at the soil line. Pull one up. The stem may be thin, twisted and brown, called wire stem. Patches often spread outward from one spot.

items: Gaps in the seedbed because seeds rotted before they sprouted.
Seedlings that fall over at the soil line, with a water soaked, thin stem.
Brown, mushy or thin, twisted stems, called wire stem.
Roots that are brown and rotted, or few and weak.
Patches of dead seedlings that spread outward from one spot in a wet tray or bed.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Cutworms also cut seedlings at the soil line. But they leave a clean cut stem and a caterpillar in the soil nearby. Damping off leaves a thin, water soaked, rotten stem and brown roots.
How Damping Off Hurts Your Crop

The sources I found give no single loss figure for the Philippines. University extension services say that within days, hundreds or thousands of seedlings can die. They add that the loss costs you the planting date as well as the seed. Waterlogged soil and poor temperatures make seedlings more open to the disease.

There is no spray threshold. The best action is to prevent it before sowing. Pull out any infected seedlings the day you see them. For pests that attack the same seedlings, see our page on [cutworms](/pests/cutworm).

items: Sterilize the seedbed soil or tray media before sowing. The Pacific Pests fact sheet suggests heat, such as an earth oven for more than an hour, or boiling water.
Use clean, well drained containers or raised beds, and use clean tools. One percent sodium hypochlorite (bleach) disinfects equipment, according to the Pacific Pests fact sheet.
Water with clean water, such as rainwater, not pond or stream water, and do not overwater.
Sow shallowly and thinly, and do not stack filled trays, since crowded, wet seedlings rot first.
Mix well rotted compost or coconut coir into the media, as the Pacific Pests fact sheet advises.
Remove sick seedlings and the soil around them at once. Treat the seed with Trichoderma, a biological control tested in several studies, before you reach for a fungicide.

blocks.text: Fungicides help only when the cultural steps fail. Seedlings can be sensitive to them, so use them on seed and seedbeds with care. The Pacific Pests fact sheet names the ingredients below. Follow the FPA registered label.

blocks.caption: Active ingredients that work. Always follow the label of an FPA registered product.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Start every season with sterilized seedbed media and clean trays.
Keep the bed well drained and water only as much as the seedlings need.
Use fresh, healthy seed and do not sow too thickly.
Write down which beds lost seedlings, and move the nursery to a new spot next time.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Damping Off

items.a: Soil living organisms, mostly Pythium and Rhizoctonia, along with Phytophthora and Fusarium. They are common in soil and strike in wet, poorly drained seedbeds.

items.q: Can I save seedlings that have fallen over?
items.a: No, a collapsed seedling will not recover. Remove it with the soil around it and fix the wetness and the drainage.

items.q: What is the best way to prevent damping off?
items.a: Start with sterilized media, good drainage, clean water and shallow sowing. Use a seed treatment only when cultural steps are not enough.
